items.title: A Euclidean sphere is a regular level set with tangent hyperplanes
items.strategy: For $F(x)=\|x\|_2^2$, compute $DF(x)h=2\langle x,h\rangle$. On $F^{-1}(R^2)$ with $R>0$, the derivative is nonzero and hence surjective to $\mathbb R$. Apply the regular-level-set theorem and identify the tangent space as $x^\perp$. Treat the empty negative level and the singular zero level separately in the discussion.

items.title: A positive-definite quadratic ellipsoid is a regular level set
items.strategy: For a symmetric positive-definite matrix $A$, set $F(x)=\langle Ax,x\rangle$. Compute $DF(x)h=2\langle Ax,h\rangle$. On the positive level $F=1$, one has $x\ne0$ and $Ax\ne0$, since $Ax=0$ would contradict positive definiteness. Thus the derivative is surjective, and the tangent hyperplane is $(Ax)^\perp$.

items.title: The graph of a $C^k$ Euclidean map is a regular level set
items.strategy: For $\psi:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$, define $G(x,y)=y-\psi(x)$. Its derivative is $DG=(-D\psi,I_n)$, which is surjective at every graph point. The regular-level-set theorem identifies $G^{-1}(0)$ with the graph, and the tangent space is $\{(v,D\psi(x)v):v\in\mathbb R^m\}$ by solving the kernel equation.

items.title: The one-sheeted hyperboloid is a regular surface of revolution
items.strategy: Use $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$. On $F^{-1}(1)$ the gradient $(2x,2y,-2z)$ cannot vanish, so the level is regular. Its equation is invariant under rotations in the $xy$-plane, and rotating the profile $x=\sqrt{1+z^2}$ around the $z$-axis gives the whole set. The tangent plane is the kernel of the displayed derivative.

items.title: The orthogonal group is a regular level set of dimension $n(n-1)/2$
items.strategy: Read $A\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}A$ as a polynomial map $\mathbb R^{n^2}\to\mathbb R^{n(n+1)/2}$, compute its derivative $H\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}H+H^{\mathsf T}A$ as a directional derivative, and solve $Df(A)H=S$ by $H=AS/2$ at a point of the fibre to get surjectivity. The graph dimension and the skew-symmetric description of the tangent space follow from the regular level set corollary.

items.title: The cone $x^2+y^2=z^2$ has a rank drop at its apex
items.strategy: Take $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$. Its zero level is the double cone. Away from the origin the gradient $(2x,2y,-2z)$ is nonzero, so the level is locally regular; at the apex the derivative is zero. Show directly that no neighbourhood of the apex in the cone is a graph over any plane by using the two nappes or the failure of a unique tangent plane.

items.title: The cusp $y^2=x^3$ has a rank drop at the origin
items.strategy: Let $F(x,y)=y^2-x^3$. Its derivative is $(-3x^2,2y)$, nonzero on the zero level except at the origin. The parametrization $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ shows the cusp and gives zero velocity at the origin; the two branches cannot form a $C^1$ graph with a regular parametrization there. This isolates the failure at the critical point.

items.title: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$ has nonconstant rank on every neighbourhood of the origin
items.strategy: Its Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\y&x\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $x$. Hence the rank is two when $x\ne0$ and one when $x=0$. Every neighbourhood of the origin meets both sets, even though the derivative is continuous and the rank-one locus itself is closed rather than open.

items.title: A critical value can have a smooth level set
items.strategy: For $F(x,y)=x^2$, zero is a critical value because every point of $F^{-1}(0)=\{x=0\}$ has nonsurjective derivative. Nevertheless the level set is the vertical line, the graph of the zero function over the $y$-axis. This separates regularity of a defining map from smoothness of the underlying set.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers locate the extrema of a linear functional on a sphere
items.strategy: For nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^m$, optimize $f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle$ subject to $G(x)=\|x\|_2^2-R^2=0$ with $R>0$. The multiplier equation is $a=2\lambda x$, so the constraint gives $x=\pm R a/\|a\|_2$. Evaluate $f$ there and use Cauchy--Schwarz to verify the global maximum and minimum. Treat $a=0$ separately as the constant objective.

items.title: Two constraints on a sphere-plane circle, where one multiplier solution is only a local maximum
items.strategy: Check that $DG$ has rank two everywhere on the circle, substitute $s=x+y$ to reduce the objective to $(s^2+2s-1)/2$ with $-\sqrt2\le s\le\sqrt2$, read off the global extrema by two elementary inequalities, use $\|p-P_4\|_2^2=2+\sqrt2 s$ to turn the $s$-range near the left end into an explicit ball, and show the fourth multiplier solution is a strict local maximum that is not global.

items.title: FALSE: every level set of a smooth map is locally a graph
items.strategy: Inline the source-backed cone witness rather than depending on the AI-generated counterexample item: for $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$, compute $DF(0)=0$ and identify $F^{-1}(0)$ as the double cone. If it were a $C^1$ graph over any plane near the apex, it would have one tangent plane there, whereas its generating rays supply incompatible tangent directions. Contrast this with the regular-level-set theorem, whose surjectivity hypothesis is exactly what is missing.

items.title: FALSE: a critical value must have a singular level set
items.strategy: Inline the source-backed witness rather than depending on the AI-generated counterexample item. For $F(x,y)=x^2$, compute $DF(x,y)=(2x,0)$, so zero is a critical value because every point of $F^{-1}(0)$ lies on the line $x=0$ and is critical. The same level is the graph of the zero function over the $y$-axis, hence a smooth line. Thus criticality prevents the regular-value theorem from applying but does not make the underlying subset singular.

items.strategy: Use $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$. Its derivative matrix has polynomial entries and is continuous, but its determinant is $x$, so its rank is one on the vertical axis and two off it. This also illustrates the correct lower-semicontinuity theorem: rank can jump upward nearby.

items.title: The rank of a derivative and constant-rank Euclidean maps
Submatrices and minors of a rectangular matrix
A matrix has rank at least $r$ exactly when it has a nonzero $r$-rowed minor
items.strategy: For $1\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$, a nonzero $r$-rowed minor has independent columns, so the ambient matrix has rank at least $r$. Conversely choose $r$ independent columns from a matrix of rank at least $r$; row rank equals column rank for the resulting $m\times r$ matrix, so some $r$ rows form a full-row-rank square submatrix. The invertible-matrix theorem makes it invertible, and its determinant is nonzero. Keep the positive-size restriction explicit so no undeclared empty determinant is used.

items.title: Differential rank is lower semicontinuous
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ map, prove that $\{x:\operatorname{rank}Df(x)\ge r\}$ is open for every positive $r$: when $r$ exceeds either the source or target dimension the locus is empty; otherwise, at a point in the set, the rank-minor lemma selects one nonzero $r$-rowed Jacobian minor, and continuity of the derivative entries and of the determinant keeps that minor nonzero nearby. The $r=0$ locus is the whole open domain. Conclude that every maximal-rank locus is open, including the empty locus.

items.title: Submersions and immersions between Euclidean open sets
Regular and critical points, regular and critical values, and level sets
The tangent space to a regular level set
A nonzero rank minor supplies the source coordinates for the constant-rank theorem
items.strategy: After permuting source and target coordinates, arrange that the leading $r\times r$ minor of $Df(a)$ is nonzero. Form $\Phi(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_r(x),x_{r+1},\ldots,x_m)$. Its derivative at $a$ is block triangular with that minor on the diagonal, so the inverse function theorem and higher-inverse regularity give a local $C^k$ diffeomorphism. Treat $r=0$ by the identity source chart and $r=m$ by the full map.

items.title: In source rank coordinates, the remaining components depend only on the rank coordinates
items.strategy: Write $g=f\circ\Phi^{-1}$, so its first $r$ components are the first $r$ coordinates. Constant rank $r$ and the rank-minor criterion force every derivative of a remaining component in a remaining source direction to vanish: otherwise adjoining that entry to the identity corner produces a nonzero $(r+1)$-rowed minor. On a small rectangular coordinate neighbourhood, zero derivative on each connected slice makes each tail component depend only on the first $r$ variables. Handle $r=0$, $r=m$, and $r=n$ separately where one coordinate block is empty.

items.title: The Euclidean constant-rank normal form
items.strategy: Use the source-coordinate lemma and write the transformed map as $(u,h(u))$. The target shear $(z,w)\mapsto(z,w-h(z))$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with an explicit inverse, and it changes the map to $(u,v)\mapsto(u,0)$. For rank zero use local constancy on a ball; for full source or target rank keep the empty coordinate block explicit. State both coordinate diffeomorphisms and their domains rather than suppressing the local restrictions.

items.title: A Euclidean submersion is locally a coordinate projection
items.strategy: At a submersion point the derivative has the maximal target rank. Lower semicontinuity therefore makes that rank constant on a neighbourhood, and the constant-rank theorem reduces the map to projection onto the first target-many coordinates. Include the equal-dimensional local-diffeomorphism case.

items.title: A Euclidean immersion is locally the canonical inclusion and is locally an embedding
items.strategy: At an immersion point the derivative has maximal source rank, which persists nearby by lower semicontinuity. The constant-rank normal form becomes $u\mapsto(u,0)$; this is injective with a continuous $C^k$ inverse from its image, so after shrinking the original map is a $C^k$ embedding onto its local image. Treat equal dimensions as the inverse-function case.

items.title: Euclidean submersions are open maps
items.strategy: For a point in the image of an open set, shrink to the local projection coordinates supplied by the submersion normal form. Coordinate diffeomorphisms and the canonical projection are open, so the image contains a neighbourhood of the selected target point. Repeat for every image point; the empty open set is immediate.

items.title: A constant-rank level set is locally a coordinate slice
items.strategy: Apply the constant-rank normal form at a point of $f^{-1}(c)$. In the resulting source coordinates the level-set equation is exactly $u=0$, while the remaining $m-r$ coordinates are free. Pull the slice back by the source diffeomorphism and state the empty level set as a vacuous case. The result is local and does not invoke unbuilt manifold terminology.

items.title: A regular level set is locally a $C^k$ graph of dimension $m-n$
items.strategy: At a point of a regular level set the derivative is surjective, so maximal target rank persists on a neighbourhood. Apply the constant-rank level-set theorem with rank $n$. Use the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition $\mathbb R^m=\ker Df(a)\oplus(\ker Df(a))^\perp$; the projection of the pulled-back slice to the kernel has invertible derivative at the point, so the inverse function theorem rewrites it as a graph over the kernel with values in the orthogonal complement. Record the vacuous empty-fibre convention and the zero-dimensional case $m=n$.

items.title: Tangent vectors to a regular level set are exactly its curve velocities
items.strategy: If a differentiable curve stays in the level set, the chain rule sends its velocity into $\ker Df(a)$, which is the defined tangent space. Conversely use the local graph representation: every kernel vector gives a straight curve in graph coordinates, and pulling it back gives a $C^1$ level-set curve with the prescribed velocity. Check the zero vector by the constant curve and both inclusions separately.

items.title: A linear functional annihilating the kernel of a surjection is a unique transpose multiple
items.strategy: Let $A:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be surjective and choose one preimage of each standard basis vector. If $\ell$ vanishes on $\ker A$, subtract the corresponding finite linear combination of those preimages from an arbitrary vector to show $\ell(v)=\lambda\cdot Av$ for the vector of their $\ell$-values. Surjectivity makes $A^T$ injective, proving uniqueness. The finite coordinate choices use no choice principle, and the cases $m,n\ge1$ match the Euclidean conventions.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers for a regular vector-valued level-set constraint
items.strategy: Let $f$ have a constrained local extremum at $a$ on $G^{-1}(c)$ and assume $DG(a)$ is surjective. Every vector in $\ker DG(a)$ is a level-set curve velocity by the tangent theorem, so the parametrized-extremum theorem makes $Df(a)$ annihilate that kernel. Apply the factorization lemma to obtain the unique $\lambda\in\mathbb R^q$ with $Df(a)v=\lambda\cdot DG(a)v$ for all $v$, equivalently $\nabla f(a)=DG(a)^T\lambda$. Distinguish necessity from sufficiency.

items.strategy:
Apply the vector-valued multiplier theorem with a one-dimensional target. The transpose of the one-row Jacobian sends the scalar multiplier to the same scalar multiple of $
abla G(a)$. The regularity hypothesis is exactly $
abla G(a)
e0$, and uniqueness follows from that nonzero vector.

before.title: Jacobi Fields Conjugate Points and the Cut Locus — Examples

items.title: Jacobi fields in euclidean space
items.statement: For every n≥0, equip R^n with its standard Euclidean metric. Let I⊂R be a nondegenerate interval, x,v∈R^n, and γ(t)=x+tv for t∈I. In the standard Cartesian trivialization, the Jacobi fields along γ are exactly J(t)=A+tB for constant vectors A,B∈R^n; the constant geodesic v=0 and n=0 are included.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 5, “Geodesics of the Model Spaces—Euclidean Space,” printed p.81 / PDF labels P97–98, lines 3393–3399: constant metric coefficients, zero Christoffel symbols, Euclidean connection and straight geodesics.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 22, Example 22.1.1, printed p.160 / PDF label P167, lines 9120–9128: the affine-line Jacobi equation and affine solution claim.

items.strategy: Write J=Σ_i j_i∂_i in the global Cartesian frame. The Euclidean metric has constant identity matrix, so the Christoffel formula gives Γ=0; the coordinate geodesic equation verifies γ, and the curvature formula gives R=0. The Jacobi equation is therefore j_i''=0 componentwise. Apply the zero-derivative-implies-constant result to each j_i' and then to j_i−tB_i, and verify conversely that every A+tB field is Jacobi. State n=0, v=0, endpoints, and choice cases.

items.title: Jacobi fields in constant sectional curvature
items.statement: Assume exactly ACω inherited through the constant-curvature tensor interface. Let (M,g) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary with constant sectional curvature K, let I be a nondegenerate interval containing 0, and let γ:I→M be a unit-speed affinely parametrized geodesic. Define s_K(t)=sin(√K t)/√K for K>0, s_0(t)=t, and s_K(t)=sinh(√(-K)t)/√(-K) for K<0. The normal Jacobi fields J with J(0)=0 are exactly J(t)=s_K(t)E(t), where E is a unique parallel normal field along γ. The tangential Jacobi fields are exactly (at+b)γ˙(t), for a,b∈R. No completeness is required; included endpoint derivatives are one-sided.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Lemma 10.8 and proof, printed pp.179–180 / PDF labels P195–196, lines 6974–7020; Lee treats constant-curvature manifolds without imposing completeness.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 24, Proposition 24.1.1 and proof, printed pp.174–175 / PDF labels P181–182, lines 9810–9848; the source assumes a complete space form, a stronger scope than this local proof.

items.strategy: Assume exactly ACω inherited through def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form and prop-curvature-tensor-of-constant-sectional-curvature; no further choice is used. Define sK and verify sK″+KsK=0, sK(0)=0, sK′(0)=1. For a parallel normal E, metric compatibility and the curvature-tensor formula give D_t²(sK E)+R(sK E,T)T=0, so sK E is a normal Jacobi field. Conversely, if J is normal Jacobi with J(0)=0, metric compatibility gives W=D_tJ(0)⊥T(0); uniquely extend W to a parallel field E, and metric compatibility plus the zero-derivative interval corollary keeps E normal. The field sK E has the same Jacobi initial data as J, so the earlier Jacobi IVP uniqueness theorem makes them equal; E is unique because E(0)=W. Tangential fields use the earlier tangential-Jacobi proposition. State all interval, one-sided endpoint, unit-speed, low-dimensional, zero-field and completeness conventions explicitly.

items.title: Conjugate antipodes on the round sphere
items.statement: Assuming countable choice through the declared proof dependencies: On a round n-sphere of radius R, n>=2, the antipode at distance pi R is conjugate along each great-circle meridian with multiplicity n-1.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: Locate the antipode as the cut-time endpoint of the radial unit-speed geodesic via the flat-sphere cut example. On the constant-curvature sphere K=1/R^2 the normal Jacobi fields vanishing at 0 are R sin(t/R)E with E a unique parallel normal field, so each w in the normal space v-perp yields an endpoint-vanishing field s_K E at t=pi R; the normal space has dimension n-1 by rank-nullity applied to w -> g(v,w). Conversely, for any endpoint-vanishing Jacobi field its pairing with the velocity is affine with two zeros, forcing the initial covariant derivative into v-perp; the initial-derivative map is injective by Jacobi initial-value uniqueness. Matching the two bounds gives multiplicity n-1. Exactly AC-omega is inherited through the constant-curvature and sphere interfaces.

items.statement: Assuming countable choice through the declared proof dependencies: a finite-dimensional boundaryless constant-curvature manifold with K<=0 has no conjugate points along any nonconstant affinely parametrized geodesic: every Jacobi field vanishing at two distinct times vanishes identically.

items.title: Killing jacobi fields from rotations
items.statement: Rotational Killing fields on a round sphere restrict to Jacobi fields along great-circle geodesics.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: Use the coordinate-plane rotation R_theta=exp(theta A) on the unit round S^n with generator X(x)=Ax. Verify explicitly that R_theta is orthogonal, preserves the sphere, satisfies the flow identities and integrates X; the rotation flow therefore consists of isometries of the round metric, so the Lie derivative of the metric along X vanishes and X is Killing. The earlier proposition then makes t->X(gamma(t)) a Jacobi field along every affinely parametrized geodesic, in particular along great circles. No choice axiom is used.

items.title: Cut locus of a point on a round sphere
items.statement: Assuming countable choice through the declared proof dependencies: On a round n-sphere of radius R with n>=2, every direction has cut time pi R and Cut(p) is the antipode.

references.title: J.-H. Eschenburg, Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry
references.locator: Section 5, Example 5.1, printed p.16: states the unit-sphere cut time but supplies no proof; the radius-R distance and cut-time calculation are proved locally here.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed p.190 (PDF P206), lines 7559-7571: finite cut-point/cut-locus convention; the sphere calculation is proved locally here.

items.strategy: Work on S_R^n as the regular level set F^{-1}(R^2) of F(x)=<x,x>: it is a nonempty connected boundaryless embedded n-manifold with T_xS_R^n = x^perp, and the induced metric is the restricted Euclidean metric. The induced connection is the tangential projection of the ambient Euclidean derivative and coincides with the Levi-Civita connection, so a curve is a geodesic exactly when its ambient acceleration is normal to the sphere. For x in S_R^n, w in T_xS_R^n and a=|w|, the explicit curve gamma(t)=cos(at/R)x+(R/a)sin(at/R)w has |gamma|=R, speed a and acceleration -(a^2/R^2)gamma normal to the sphere; hence it is the unique maximal geodesic (w=0 gives the constant geodesic), the sphere is geodesically complete, and Hopf-Rinow makes it metrically complete. Lower bound: for a piecewise-C^1 path alpha from p to q, u=<p,alpha>/R^2 satisfies |u|<=1, <alpha,alpha-dot>=0 and |u-prime|<=sqrt(1-u^2)|alpha-dot|/R; regularizing by theta_eps=arccos((1-eps)u) gives |theta_eps-prime|<=|alpha-dot|/R, and integrating with the vector FTC/norm inequality and letting eps go to 0 yields L_g(alpha)>=R arccos(<p,q>/R^2). Upper bound: with theta=arccos(<p,q>/R^2), the unit direction v=(q-cos(theta)p)/(R sin(theta)) in p^perp gives the unit-speed geodesic reaching q in length R theta, the endpoint cases theta=0 and theta=pi being handled separately (the latter needs a unit vector in p^perp, which exists because n>=2). Hence d_g(p,q)=R arccos(<p,q>/R^2), and along every unit radial geodesic the minimizing times are exactly (0,pi R], so c_p(v)=pi R and each cut endpoint is gamma_v(pi R)=-p, that is, Cut(p)={-p}. Only the declared AC_omega is used, through the induced-connection, maximal-geodesic, Hopf-Rinow and cut-time interfaces; no curvature computation is required.

items.title: Cut locus of a point on a flat circle
items.statement: Assuming exactly the declared countable-choice hypothesis: For every L>0 and p=[x] in the flat circle C_L=R/(LZ) with period-coordinate metric dx^2, the two unit directions have cut time L/2 and Cut(p) is the antipode [x+L/2]. At the cut point the two opposite semicircles are minimizing.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997), Chapter 10
references.locator: Printed p.190 (PDF P206), lines 7559-7571: cut-time definition and flat-cylinder example; the circle quotient-distance and cut-time calculation are derived locally.

items.strategy: Construct the flat quotient circle in period coordinates and check it is nonempty, connected, boundaryless, and geodesically complete; Hopf-Rinow gives metric completeness under exactly AC_omega. Lift any piecewise-C1 competitor through the period covering. Its endpoint differs from a chosen lift by an integer period, and the Euclidean length bound gives a lower bound by the smallest such displacement. A floor argument attains the nearest-period minimum, while projected straight segments attain the bound. The distance formula makes the minimizing-time set along either unit radial ray exactly (0,L/2], with two tied semicircles at the endpoint and strict failure afterwards; the two directions have the same antipodal endpoint. The torus computation belongs to its separately assigned example.

items.title: Cut locus on a flat rectangular torus from the dirichlet cell
items.statement: Assume exactly ACω through the declared geodesic, Hopf–Rinow, cut-time, and cut-locus dependencies. Let a,b>0, Λ=aZ×bZ, Q=R²/Λ with its quotient flat metric, and p=[x₀]∈Q. Under the period-coordinate identification TₚQ≅R², define the radial tangent cut domain including zero by Cₚ={0}∪{tu: |u|=1, 0<t<cₚ(u)}. Then Cₚ=D°=(-a/2,a/2)×(-b/2,b/2); equivalently, the positive tangent cut domain is D°∖{0}. For each unit u=(u₁,u₂), cₚ(u)=min{a/(2|u₁|):u₁≠0}∪{b/(2|u₂|):u₂≠0}. For D=[-a/2,a/2]×[-b/2,b/2], Cut(p)={ [x₀+w]:w∈∂D }. Opposite edges are identified; relative interiors of edges have two nearest lattice lifts, and the corner class has four.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997), Chapter 10
references.locator: Printed p.190 / PDF P206, lines 7559–7568: Lee defines cut points and cut loci and gives the flat-cylinder halfway example; the rectangular-torus distance and Dirichlet-cell calculation are proved locally in this item.

items.strategy: Construct the quotient smooth flat metric using small periodic charts. For any two classes, lift every piecewise-C¹ path from a fixed representative; its endpoint is a lattice translate, and the Euclidean vector-valued FTC plus the norm inequality bounds length below by that endpoint displacement. Coordinatewise integer-part rounding attains a nearest lattice translate, while its projected straight segment attains that length; hence d([x],[y])=min_{λ∈Λ}|y−x+λ|. The constant chart metric has zero Christoffel symbols, so all geodesics are global affine projections and Hopf–Rinow gives completeness under the stated ACω. In the closed product Dirichlet rectangle, zero is a nearest lattice point; outside it, shifting a coordinate by its period strictly shortens the radial lift. Compute the first boundary-exit time of each unit ray, prove the tangent cut domain and cut locus by both inclusions, and count the nearest lifts on faces and corners.

items.title: A cut point that is not conjugate because two minimizers arrive
items.statement: Assuming exactly ACω through the declared circle example: on a flat circle of circumference L>0, the antipode of p is a cut point reached by two distinct minimizing semicircles, but p and the antipode are not conjugate along either semicircle. Thus a cut point need not be conjugate along a minimizing geodesic reaching it.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed p.190 / PDF label P206, lines 7559–7571: Lee notes that the flat cylinder has no conjugate points and geodesics wrapping more than halfway are not minimizing; the circle witness is calculated locally here.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Appendix C.14.2, printed p.278 / PDF labels P284–285, lines 14021–14050: Klingenberg statement and an exercise outline linking nonconjugate cut points with two minimizing geodesics; this local example does not rely on the exercise.

items.strategy: Use the earlier flat-circle example for the antipodal cut point and the two explicit minimizing semicircles. In a period chart the metric coefficient is constant, so the Christoffel symbols and hence the curvature vanish; the coordinate field is a parallel frame, the Jacobi equation reduces to j″=0, and the Euclidean-affine solutions j=a+bt with j(0)=j(L/2)=0 force j=0 because L/2>0. Nonzero endpoint-vanishing Jacobi fields therefore do not exist, and the conjugacy definition makes the cut point nonconjugate along both minimizers. Exactly ACω is inherited only to invoke the circle example; the local Jacobi calculation uses no choice.

items.title: A conjugate point at which there are many geodesics
items.statement: On the round sphere S_R^n of radius R>0 with n>=2, for every unit v in T_pS_R^n the radial geodesic gamma_v(t)=exp_p(tv) on [0,pi R] is a minimizing geodesic from p to the antipode -p along which -p is conjugate to p with multiplicity n-1; the unit directions give infinitely many pairwise distinct such meridians. So a conjugate point need not be the endpoint of a unique minimizing geodesic: the explicit N-indexed family is built from one orthonormal pair of tangent directions and refutes the uniqueness claim assumed in the Statement refuted.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.189-190: conjugate points, the cut locus as last minimizing instant, and the round-sphere comparison; the infinite family is computed locally.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)

items.title: Tangential jacobi fields are affine multiples of the velocity
items.statement: Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold, I a nondegenerate interval, gamma an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic, and f smooth and real-valued. If gamma is nonconstant, f gamma-dot is Jacobi if and only if f(t)=at+b on I for constants a,b. If gamma is constant, f gamma-dot is the zero Jacobi field for every smooth f. items.title: Killing fields restrict to jacobi fields along geodesics
items.statement: Let (M,g) be a smooth boundaryless Riemannian manifold and X a smooth vector field whose maximal local flow is Phi. Define X to be Killing when L_X g=0. Each compact subinterval uses a common local-flow time interval; included endpoints use one-sided derivatives. No completeness is required.

items.title: Conjugate points along a geodesic and their multiplicity
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional n-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) without boundary, a<b and an affinely parametrized geodesic γ:[a,b]→M, let Kγ(a,b) be the real vector space of smooth Jacobi fields along γ that vanish at both endpoints. This space is finite-dimensional. The endpoints are conjugate along γ iff Kγ(a,b) contains a nonzero field; the multiplicity of a conjugate pair is dim_R Kγ(a,b). If γ is constant then Kγ(a,b)={0}; if γ is nonconstant then dim_R Kγ(a,b)≤n−1. Included endpoints use one-sided derivatives. No completeness or choice axiom is required.

items.title: Conjugate instants are isolated unless the geodesic is constant
items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used through [[lem-wronskian-of-two-jacobi-fields-is-constant]]. Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior, let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic, and fix $a\in I$. Define $$C_a(\gamma):=\{t\in I:t>a\text{ and }\gamma(a),\gamma(t)\text{ are conjugate along }\gamma|_{[a,t]}\}.$$ If $\gamma$ is nonconstant, then $C_a(\gamma)$ is discrete in $I\cap(a,\infty)$, and every compact subinterval of $I\cap(a,\infty)$ meets $C_a(\gamma)$ in finitely many points. If $\gamma$ is constant, then $C_a(\gamma)=\varnothing$. No completeness or full Axiom of Choice is assumed. At included endpoints, discreteness is relative to the parameter interval and derivatives are one-sided.

items.title: Conjugate points and multiplicity are invariant under affine reparametrization

Hence conjugacy is equivalent in both directions and multiplicities agree; a negative slope exchanges the endpoints. Constant geodesics and dimension zero are included.

items.title: Second variation formula for energy
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega through the Riemann-tensor symmetry dependency: Let F(s,r,t) be an admissible two-parameter variation on a compact interval [a,b] with a<b, smooth on a common finite subdivision in t and smooth in (s,r) at the seams, whose central curve gamma(t)=F(0,0,t) is an affinely parametrized geodesic. Put E(s,r)=1/2 integral_a^b |F_t|^2 dt, V=F_s(0,0,.), W=F_r(0,0,.), T=gamma-dot. Then partial_s partial_r E(0,0)=integral_a^b (g(D_tV,D_tW)-g(R(V,T)T,W))dt+[g(D_sW,T)]_a^b. Equivalently, after piecewise integration by parts this is [g(D_sW,T)]_a^b+[g(D_tV,W)]_a^b-sum_j g(Delta_j D_tV,W(t_j))-integral_a^b g(D_t^2V+R(V,T)T,W)dt. Here Delta_j is the right-minus-left covariant-derivative jump. If endpoints are fixed, the acceleration term vanishes (and W(a)=W(b)=0 in the integrated form).

items.title: Index form of a geodesic segment
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega as propagated through the declared second-variation and Riemann-symmetry dependencies: Let a<b and let gamma:[a,b]->M be an affinely parametrized geodesic. Let X_pw^1(gamma) be the real vector space of continuous vector fields along gamma that are C1 on each piece of some finite subdivision, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. Define I_gamma(V,W)=integral_a^b (g(D_tV,D_tW)-g(R(V,gamma-dot)gamma-dot,W))dt, using finite piecewise Riemann integration. This is a symmetric bilinear form. Its fixed-endpoint subspace is X_0(gamma)={V in X_pw^1(gamma): V(a)=V(b)=0}. For every fixed-endpoint two-parameter variation with central gamma, the mixed energy derivative equals I_gamma(V,W).

items.statement: Assume ACω as carried by the supplied index-form definition and def-countable-choice. Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold, a<b, and γ:[a,b]→M an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic. Fix a finite subdivision a=t₀<⋯<tₘ=b and continuous fields V,W along γ, with V C² and W C¹ on each closed piece. Define ΔⱼD_tV=D_tV(tⱼ⁺)−D_tV(tⱼ⁻). Then Iγ(V,W)=[g(D_tV,W)]ₐᵇ−Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ⁻¹g(ΔⱼD_tV,W(tⱼ))−Σₖ₌₁ᵐ∫ₜₖ₋₁ᵗₖg(D_t²V+R(V,T)T,W)dt, where T=γ̇ and the outer bracket uses one-sided endpoint traces. The finite-piece calculation adds no further choice assumption.

items.title: Jacobi fields are the null solutions of the index form with fixed endpoints

Let γ:[a,b]→M be an affinely parametrized geodesic with a<b, and let X²_pw(γ) be the continuous fields that are C² on every piece of some finite subdivision; set X²_0=X²_pw∩{V:V(a)=V(b)=0}. The radical of Iγ restricted to X²_0 is exactly the Jacobi fields with J(a)=J(b)=0. For any smooth Jacobi field J, Iγ(J,W)=0 for every unconstrained continuous piecewise-C¹ test field W if and only if D_tJ(a)=D_tJ(b)=0. items.title: Index lemma
items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited countable-choice axiom AC_omega. Let (M,g) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, a<b, and gamma:[a,b]->M an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic with T=gamma-dot. Assume that for no t in (a,b] are gamma(a),gamma(t) conjugate along gamma|[a,t]. Let u in T_{gamma(a)}M and w in T_{gamma(b)}M. Then (1) there is exactly one Jacobi field J along gamma with J(a)=u and J(b)=w; (2) for every continuous field V along gamma that is C^1 on the pieces of a finite subdivision and satisfies V(a)=u, V(b)=w, one has I_gamma(J,J)<=I_gamma(V,V), with equality if and only if V=J. Constant geodesics, dimension zero, u=w=0 and non-unit speed are included; no completeness, compactness or full AC.

For V=J+W with W zero at both endpoints, integration by parts with the Jacobi equation cancels I(J,W). In a parallel frame the fields J_i=J_{E_i(a)} form a basis, W=A f, and the Wronskian identity <A-prime g, A h>=<A g, A-prime h> turns the integrand into <A f-prime, A f-prime> plus the exact derivative d/dt<A-prime f, A f>. Because A(t)=(t-a)(I+o(1)) and W(a)=0 the boundary term at a vanishes in the limit, so I(W,W)=integral of <A f-prime,A f-prime> >=0; equality forces f-prime=0, hence f constant and zero by W(b)=0.

items.title: H-one Riemannian curves and their half-energy
items.statement: Under AC_omega, on a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, an H1 curve on [a,b] is a continuous curve with a finite chart subdivision whose coordinate representatives are L2-derivative primitives; it has an a.e. tangent velocity, intrinsic L1 length and half-energy E=1/2 integral |alpha-dot|_g^2, and the H1 path topology implies uniform convergence. Smooth composition obeys the a.e. L2 chain rule.

items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited countable-choice axiom AC_omega, propagated through the declared exponential-map, Jacobi-field and conjugacy suppliers. Let (M,g) be a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, let a<b, and let gamma:[a,b]->M be an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic such that for no t in (a,b] are gamma(a) and gamma(t) conjugate along gamma|[a,t]. Write p=gamma(a), v=gamma-dot(a), X=(b-a)v. Then there is a real epsilon>0 such that every continuous piecewise C^1 curve gamma-bar:[a,b]->M with gamma-bar(a)=gamma(a), gamma-bar(b)=gamma(b) and sup_t d_g(gamma-bar(t),gamma(t))<epsilon satisfies L_g(gamma-bar)>=L_g(gamma), and equality holds if and only if gamma-bar=gamma@tau for some continuous nondecreasing piecewise C^1 surjection tau:[a,b]->[a,b] with tau(a)=a and tau(b)=b. The piecewise integration-by-parts identity gives I(V,V)=0 and I(V,W)=-|D_tJ(c^-)|^2. For a sufficiently small positive δ, X=V+δW has I(X,X)<0. Realize X by the explicit fixed-endpoint piecewise smooth variation β(s,t)=exp_{γ(t)}(sX(t)); compactness and openness of the exponential domain give one common parameter interval, including matching parameter derivatives at the seam. The differential of exp at the zero section is the identity, so β_s-field is X. First variation gives E′(0)=0, second variation gives E″(0)=I(X,X)<0, and the second-derivative test yields E(β_s)<E(γ) for small nonzero s. Since γ has constant speed, L(γ)^2=2(b-a)E(γ); the length-energy inequality gives L(β_s)^2≤2(b-a)E(β_s)<L(γ)^2. This direct argument is local and needs no completeness.

items.title: At a conjugate endpoint the index form is degenerate
items.statement: Assume exactly AC_omega through the declared dependencies. (a) If gamma(a) and gamma(b) are conjugate along an affinely parametrized geodesic gamma:[a,b]->M (a<b, finite-dimensional boundaryless), then the fixed-endpoint index form on X_0(gamma) is degenerate: some nonzero J in X_0(gamma) satisfies I_gamma(J,W)=0 for every W in X_0(gamma). (b) On the round sphere S_R^n (R>0, n>=2), for p and unit v, gamma(t)=exp_p(tv) on [0,pi R] ends at -p, is minimizing with d(p,-p)=L(gamma)=pi R, but is not a strict local minimizer: for every epsilon>0 there is a piecewise C^1 path sigma != gamma from p to -p with L(sigma)=pi R and sup_t d(sigma(t),gamma(t))<epsilon. The fixed-endpoint index form is degenerate with nullspace exactly the endpoint-vanishing Jacobi fields, of dimension n-1.

items.strategy: Read degeneracy off the endpoint-vanishing Jacobi field via integration by parts; on the sphere compare the radial geodesic with the family of meridians through the antipode, all of length pi R and uniformly close. Do not claim that every conjugate endpoint fails to minimize.

items.title: Cut time in a unit tangent direction
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, for complete connected boundaryless M and unit v in T_pM, c(v)=sup{t>0:d(p,exp_p(tv))=t} in (0,infinity], with infinity allowed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: Hopf-Rinow makes the radial exponential global; local normal minimization makes the set nonempty. The supremum is an extended real, and n=0 has no unit directions.

items.title: Minimizing along a geodesic is an initial interval property
items.statement: Assuming countable choice through the declared proof dependencies: For a complete connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold, p in M, unit v in T_pM, and gamma(t)=exp_p(tv), the minimizing-time set A_p(v)={t>=0:d_g(p,gamma(t))=t} is an initial interval; moreover, if the cut time c_p(v) is finite, then c_p(v) belongs to A_p(v). Equivalently, once an earlier segment fails to minimize, no later segment along this ray minimizes.

references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: A shorter competitor to the earlier endpoint, concatenated with the remaining geodesic tail, shortens any later radial segment. Continuity of distance makes the equality set closed at a finite supremum.

items.title: Cut point and cut locus of a point
items.statement: Assuming countable choice through the declared proof dependencies: For a complete connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, let S_pM={v in T_pM: |v|=1}. Define Cut(p)={exp_p(c_p(v)v): v in S_pM and c_p(v)<infinity}; each such endpoint is the first cut point along its specified radial geodesic, and Cut(p) is empty when S_pM is empty.

references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

items.strategy: Use finite attainment from item 25, the global exponential domain and the empty-sphere convention in dimension zero.

items.title: Unit spheres in finite-dimensional normed spaces are sequentially compact
items.statement: No choice principle is used. Let V be a finite-dimensional real normed space with unit sphere S = {v in V : ||v|| = 1}. Then S is sequentially compact: every sequence in S has a subsequence converging in the norm metric to a point of S. Consequently, for a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the unit sphere S_pM = {v in T_pM : |v|_g = 1} is sequentially compact, so every sequence of unit tangent vectors at p has a subsequence converging in the norm metric of T_pM to a unit tangent vector at p. Dimension zero and dimension one are included.
items.strategy: The closed unit ball of a finite-dimensional normed space is compact because a finite basis gives a coordinate isomorphism; compactness passes to countably compact and then sequentially compact subspaces, and the limit of a sequence of unit vectors is again a unit vector by the reverse triangle inequality.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: Closed unit ball of a finite-dimensional normed space

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lemma 23.2.2 proof, printed pp.167-168, limiting-direction subsequence

items.title: The pointwise norm on a tangent space is smooth off the zero vector
items.statement: No choice principle is used. Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with n = dim M in N and p in M. Then the pointwise norm N_p(w) = |w|_g = sqrt(g_p(w,w)) is smooth on T_pM minus the zero vector; in the canonical linear coordinates of any ordered basis of T_pM the coordinate representative sqrt(q(lambda)) of the positive definite quadratic form q(lambda) = sum c_ij lambda_i lambda_j is smooth off the origin, and smoothness is independent of the basis.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the radial function in exponential coordinates sends q to |exp_p^{-1}(q)|_{g_p}, whose smoothness off the origin rests on the elementary tangent-space fact isolated here.

references.locator: Lecture 23, section 23.3, printed pp.170-172: differentiability of the distance function is reduced to smoothness of the tangent-space norm away from the origin.

items.title: Characterization of a cut point
items.statement: Assume exactly the countable-choice axiom AC_omega. Let (M,g) be a complete, connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, p in M, v in S_pM a unit tangent vector, gamma(t)=exp_p(tv), and c=c_p(v) in (0,+infinity] the cut time. (a) Forward: if c<infinity, then either gamma(0)=p and gamma(c) are conjugate along gamma|[0,c], or there is a unit-speed minimizing geodesic sigma:[0,c]->M with sigma(0)=p, sigma(c)=gamma(c) and sigma'(0)!=v, so two distinct minimizing geodesics join p to gamma(c) in time c. (b) Converse: (1) if t>0 and gamma(0),gamma(t) are conjugate along gamma|[0,t], then c<=t; (2) if a unit-speed minimizing sigma:[0,t]->M with sigma(0)=p, sigma(t)=gamma(t) and sigma'(0)!=v exists, then c<=t. Hence for finite c, c is the least positive instant at which one of the two forward alternatives occurs. Dimension zero is vacuous (no unit tangent vector); gamma is nonconstant because |v|_g=1.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: Minimizing geodesics to the points just beyond the cut time have lengths converging to c and unit initial directions in the sequentially compact sphere S_pM; a different limiting direction gives a second minimizing geodesic, the same direction makes exp_p identify two distinct points near cv, so exp_p is not a local diffeomorphism and the endpoints are conjugate by the critical-value theorem. Conversely, conjugacy at t gives a strictly shorter competitor past t, and a second unit-speed minimizer makes the concatenated broken path globally shortest, so its arclength representative is an unbroken geodesic and velocity uniqueness forces the two geodesics to coincide.

items.title: Cut time is positive and continuous
items.statement: Under exactly the inherited AC_omega, for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the cut time c_p: S_pM -> (0,+infinity] is (a) positive, (b) continuous in the extended topology (if c(v) is finite then c(u) -> c(v) as u -> v; if c(v)=+infinity then c(u) -> +infinity), and (c) uniformly positive: inf over S_pM of c_p is > 0 whenever S_pM is nonempty, that infimum being +infinity exactly when c is identically +infinity. Dimension zero is vacuous and no compactness of M is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the cut time as a continuous positive function of the unit direction; the two semicontinuity arguments and the uniform-positivity consequence are carried out locally here.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, section 23.2, printed pp.163-170: cut locus, Lemmas 23.2.1-23.2.2 and regularity of the distance function; the local-invertibility argument for lower semicontinuity follows the proof strategy there.

items.strategy: Upper semicontinuity: for t below a hypothetical bigger limes superior, the radial segments stay minimizing and the distance equality passes to the limit by continuity of exp_p and of the distance, contradicting the defining supremum. Lower semicontinuity: if directions u_n -> v had c(u_n) < t < c(v), Hopf-Rinow minimizers w_n to the endpoints converge (unit-sphere compactness), and the limit either identifies with tv - contradicting the injectivity of exp_p on a local-diffeomorphism neighbourhood, which exists because d(exp_p)_{tv} cannot be singular without forcing c(v) <= t through the conjugate-instant converse - or produces a second minimizing geodesic to gamma_v(t), which the two-minimizer converse bounds by c(v) <= t. Uniform positivity follows from lower semicontinuity and sequential compactness of the unit sphere.

items.title: Cut time does not exceed first conjugate time
items.statement: Under exactly the inherited AC_omega, along a unit radial geodesic gamma(t)=exp_p(tv) in a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, every positive conjugate instant t (gamma(0),gamma(t) conjugate along gamma restricted to [0,t]) satisfies cut time c_p(v)<=t; consequently, when the set C of positive conjugate instants is nonempty, c_p(v)<=inf C, the first conjugate time (no attainment of the infimum is asserted; c=+infinity forces C empty).

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, pp.173-190

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lectures 21-24, pp.153-176

items.strategy: Apply clause (b)(1) of thm-characterization-of-a-cut-point to each positive conjugate instant: every t in C satisfies c<=t, so c is a lower bound of C and is finite whenever C is nonempty. Since C is a nonempty subset of (0,infinity), bounded below by 0, thm-infimum-property supplies inf C and the greatest-lower-bound property of def-infimum gives c<=inf C. The empty-C case is vacuous, and no converse or attainment is claimed.

items.title: Injectivity radius is the infimum of cut times
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, on a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold the injectivity radius at p equals inf_{v in S_pM} c(v), an identity of extended numbers in (0,+infinity]; in dimension zero the sphere is empty, the infimum over it is +infinity by convention, and inj(p)=+infinity as computed directly from the definition. No compactness of M is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the injectivity radius at a point and its comparison with the cut locus.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, sections 23.2-23.3, printed pp.163-172: cut locus and Definition 23.3.3 of the injectivity radius.

items.strategy: Admissible radii are exactly the radii below every cut time. A radius exceeding a finite cut time is defeated either by a conjugate vector (the differential of exp_p is singular there) or by a competing minimizing geodesic (two distinct vectors in the ball with the same image), so the injectivity radius is at most the infimum of the cut times. Conversely, strictly below the infimum every point of the ball is nonconjugate and two radial minimizers are impossible, so exp_p restricted to the ball is an injective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism onto its image; completeness supplies the global exponential domain via Hopf-Rinow. The dimension-zero case is computed directly from the definition. The comparison is carried out in the extended reals, inf empty = +infinity.

items.title: Exp p is a diffeomorphism from the open tangent cut domain onto m minus the cut locus and p
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the tangent cut domain D_p={tv: v in S_pM, 0<t<c_p(v)} is open in T_pM and exp_p restricts to a diffeomorphism from D_p onto the open submanifold M minus ({p} union Cut(p)); in dimension zero both sides are empty. No compactness of M is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the domain on which exp_p is a diffeomorphism and its relation to the cut locus.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, sections 23.2-23.3, printed pp.163-172: cut time, cut locus, and the diffeomorphism domain of exp_p.

items.strategy: D_p is open because a sequence outside it cannot converge to a point of it: cut times of nearby directions stay above the length of the limit vector by continuity of the cut time, in both the finite and the infinite case. Strictly below the cut time there is no conjugate point, so exp_p is a local diffeomorphism throughout D_p; strictly below the cut time no second minimizing direction can reach the same point, so exp_p is injective on D_p. Hopf-Rinow supplies a minimizing direction to every q, and q outside the cut locus and different from p must lie strictly before its cut time, giving surjectivity with image exactly M minus ({p} union Cut(p)). The cut locus is closed, so the target is open, and a bijective local diffeomorphism onto an open submanifold is a diffeomorphism.

items.title: Distance from p is smooth off p and the cut locus
items.statement: Assuming countable choice: for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the distance function r_p(q)=d_g(p,q) is smooth on the open set M minus ({p} union Cut(p)), and in inverse exponential polar coordinates r_p(exp_p(tv))=t for every unit v and every 0<t<c_p(v), equivalently r_p(exp_p(w))=|w|_g for every w in the tangent cut domain. Dimension zero is vacuous; no compactness is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the cut-locus discussion and the radial coordinate r(q)=|exp_p^{-1}(q)|_{g_p} on M minus the cut locus.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, sections 23.2-23.3, printed pp.163-172: the tangent cut domain and differentiability of the distance function off p and the cut locus.

items.strategy: On the domain U of the global exponential diffeomorphism exp_p|D_p, the distance is the tangent-space norm of the inverse exponential coordinate: for 0<t<c_p(v) the supremum definition of the cut time, the initial-interval lemma and the epsilon characterization of the supremum give d(p,exp_p(tv))=t, while |tv|_g=t by homogeneity and |v|_g=1; hence r_p=N_p composed with (exp_p|D_p)^{-1}, a composite of smooth maps because the norm is smooth off the zero vector (local supplier lem-the-pointwise-norm-is-smooth-off-the-zero-vector).

items.title: Gradient of the distance is the outward unit radial field off the cut locus
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g), p in M, a unit v in S_pM and 0<t<c_p(v), the gradient of r_p at exp_p(tv) is the terminal velocity of the radial geodesic gamma_{p,v}, equal to d(exp_p)_{tv}(v), and it has pointwise norm one. The segment is the minimizing radial geodesic from p to exp_p(tv); dimension zero is vacuous and no compactness is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the distance function and geodesics before the cut point; polar coordinates and the radial field.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Corollary 18.1.3 and its proof, printed pp.135-136: polar normal coordinates and the identity grad r = partial_r with unit norm (the library item cor-polar-form-of-the-metric-in-normal-coordinates derives the same identity at this locator); Section 23.2, printed pp.167-169: the radial domain before the cut locus.

items.strategy: Differentiate the identity r_p composed with exp_p = N_p on the open tangent cut domain: the chain rule and the derivative g_p(w_0,X)/|w_0| of the pointwise norm along lines give d(r_p)_q(d(exp_p)_{w_0}(X)) = g_p(v,X) for every X in T_pM. Gauss lemma gives g_q(d(exp_p)_{w_0}(v), d(exp_p)_{w_0}(X)) = g_p(v,X), the differential of the diffeomorphism exp_p|D_p is a linear isomorphism onto T_qM, and the pairing identity against every tangent vector characterizes the gradient; X=v gives unit norm. The base point w_0=tv is nonzero, so the norm is differentiated only off zero, and the scale factor t cancels because d(exp_p)_{w_0}(w_0)=t d(exp_p)_{w_0}(v).

items.title: Hessian of distance in terms of radial jacobi fields
items.statement: Assuming countable choice: for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, p in M, unit v in S_pM and 0<t<c_p(v), every X in T_qM orthogonal to T=gamma-dot(t) is the endpoint of exactly one normal Jacobi field J_X along gamma with J_X(0)=0 and J_X(t)=X, and the radial endpoint map {v}^perp -> T^perp, W -> d(exp_p)_{tv}(tW), is a linear isomorphism; the Hessian of r_p satisfies (Hess r_p)_q(X,Y)=g_q(D_tJ_X(t),Y) and vanishes on the radial direction; the normal shape operator is S=D_tJ(t) circ J(t)^{-1} on T^perp and 0 on T, in the def-shape-operator sign convention the shape operator of the distance sphere is minus that, and its second fundamental form is II(X,Y)=-g_q(D_tJ_X(t),Y) nu. Dimension zero is vacuous and no compactness is assumed.

references.title: J.-H. Eschenburg, Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry
references.locator: Section 2, printed pp.6-9 (PDF labels P7-P9): for a unit gradient field $V=\\nabla f$ the operator $A=DV=D\\nabla f$ is the Hessian of $f$ and its restriction to a level hypersurface is that hypersurface's shape operator, while Jacobi fields in the equidistant family satisfy $J'=AJ$; Section 5, Lemma 5.3 and display (5.11), printed p.19 (PDF label P19): $d(\\exp_p)_{tv}e_i=J_i(t)/t$; Section 6, printed p.21 (PDF label P21): for the distance function $\\rho$ the radial field $V=\\nabla\\rho$ is unit and $D\\nabla\\rho$ vanishes on $\\mathbb R V$.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997), Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190 (PDF labels P189-P206): Jacobi fields, the differential of the exponential map as the endpoint value of a Jacobi field vanishing at $p$ (printed p.184), and the index-form material.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, section 23.2, printed pp.167-169 (PDF labels P174-P176): the cut locus, regularity of the distance and $\\nabla\\rho_p$ as the unit radial field; Lectures 21-22, printed pp.153-166: Jacobi fields and the differential of the exponential map.

items.strategy: Vary the unit direction: normalize v+sW, let F(s,tau)=exp_p(tau t v(s)); its variation field is partial_s F(0,tau)=d(exp_p)_{tau tv}(tau tW)=J_W(tau t) by the endpoint formula for Jacobi fields. Torsion-freeness, expressed by symmetric Christoffel symbols in a chart, gives D_s partial_tau F=D_tau partial_s F, so nabla_X grad r_p=D_t J_X(t). The Gauss lemma makes the endpoint map a linear isomorphism {v}^perp -> T^perp, the Wronskian makes D_tJ(t) circ J(t)^{-1} g-self-adjoint, and the radial component vanishes by unit-speed geodesicity; the shape-operator and second-fundamental-form signs follow the def-shape-operator convention.

items.title: Cut locus of a point is closed
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, on a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold the cut locus Cut(p) of a point p is closed in the metric space (M,d_g); in dimension zero the unit sphere and the cut locus are empty. No compactness of M is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, Chapter 10
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the cut locus of a point and its point-set behaviour.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, sections 23.2-23.3, printed pp.163-172: the cut locus and the continuity of the cut time.

items.strategy: Sequential closedness. A convergent sequence of cut points has cut times equal to the distances to p, hence bounded; the finite-dimensional unit sphere is sequentially compact, so a subsequence of directions converges to a unit vector; continuity of the cut time makes the limiting cut time finite and equal to d(p,q); continuity of the exponential map on the global exponential domain supplied by Hopf-Rinow identifies the limit with the cut point of the limiting direction. The metric-space equivalence between closedness and sequential closedness concludes. Countable choice is spent selecting the directions and in that equivalence.

items.title: Cut locus of a point has riemannian volume zero
items.statement: Assuming countable choice: for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the cut locus Cut(p) has zero Riemannian volume; in dimension zero Cut(p) is empty and the value is zero. No compactness of M is assumed.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190: the cut locus of a point as the radial image of the cut-time graph over the unit tangent sphere, and its closedness.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Lecture 23, section 23.3, printed pp.170-171: Corollary 23.3.2 states that the cut locus has measure zero; the local proof replaces its Rademacher/Sard route by the radial-graph, content-zero and density-chart argument.

items.strategy: The cut time is continuous on the finite-dimensional unit sphere; the 2n graph parametrisations of the sphere exhibit the radial cut-time graph as a countable union of compact content-zero sets, which the smooth cone map (x,t)->t psi(x) pushes to null sets in R^n. Hopf-Rinow makes exp_p a smooth map on all of T_pM, so the equidimensional C^1 image theorem makes Cut(p) null in M; a countable smooth atlas reduces this to chartwise Euclidean nullity, and the density chart formula plus the null-set integral theorem convert chartwise nullity into vol_g(Cut(p))=0.

items.title: Polar integration may discard the cut locus
items.statement: Assuming countable choice: for a complete connected boundaryless finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, (a) the integral of every nonnegative Borel function, and of every integrable real or complex Borel function, against the Riemannian volume equals its integral over M minus Cut(p), and in dimension zero Cut(p) is empty so the identity is trivial; (b) for n=dim M>=1 one has, for every nonnegative Borel f, the exponential polar formula integral_M f dvol_g = integral_{S_pM} integral_0^{c_p(v)} f(gamma_v(t)) det a_v(t) dt dsigma_p(v), where the inner integral is over the open interval (0,c_p(v)); a_v(t) is the matrix g(J_i(t),E_j(t)) of the normal Jacobi fields J_i with J_i(0)=0 and D_tJ_i(0)=e_i for an orthonormal basis e_i of v-perp in the parallel normal frame E_j, det a_v(t) is independent of the basis, positive for 0<t<c_p(v), and equals 1 in the empty (n=1) case; sigma_p is the polar surface measure transported from S^{n-1} by a linear isometry and independent of the isometry; the polar identity is not asserted in dimension zero, where vol_g is counting measure and the case is recorded separately.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry (2025)
references.locator: Section 27.2, 'The volume element in polar coordinates', printed pp.200-202 (PDF labels P208-P210): display (27.1) and Lemma 27.2.1 with its proof express the polar density of exp_p as the determinant of normal Jacobi fields in a parallel frame; Section 23.2 printed pp.167-170 (cut locus and the diffeomorphism property of exp_p on the tangent cut domain) and Section 23.3 printed pp.171-172 (differentiability of the distance); Section 22.3 printed pp.163-164 (conjugate points).

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed pp.173-190 (Jacobi fields, conjugate points, the differential of the exponential map, and the cut locus).

references.title: Gerald B. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed.
references.locator: Theorem 2.49 (polar coordinates) and Proposition 2.23 (countable additivity of indefinite integrals).

items.strategy: Discard the null complement {p} union Cut(p) (cut locus null by the volume-zero theorem, singleton null via a chart) so the integral may be taken over the open set U on which exp_p is a diffeomorphism onto M minus ({p} union Cut(p)); in the resulting normal chart the Riemannian density is sqrt(det G). Choose an orthonormal basis, transport the polar surface measure (independence of the isometry proved by orthogonal invariance) and reduce to a Euclidean polar integral over the open polar domain. Gauss's lemma in the adapted frame (v together with an orthonormal basis of v-perp) makes the Gram matrix block diagonal with blocks 1 and t^{-2} a a^T, so sqrt(det G) t^{n-1} = det a on 0<t<c_p(v); positivity of det a follows from non-vanishing via conjugacy and the intermediate value theorem. Tonelli swaps the iterated integrals and the transported spherical integral is rewritten over S_pM. All degenerate, endpoint, dimension-zero and choice cases are audited, AC_omega being inherited through the declared suppliers.

items.title: The Morse index theorem for geodesics
items.statement: The classical Morse index theorem is recorded as orientation only, neither proved nor consumed anywhere in this pair: the index of a geodesic segment, the maximum dimension of a linear space of proper fixed-endpoint vector fields on which the index form is negative definite, is finite and equals the number of its interior conjugate points counted with multiplicity. The finite-variation consequences actually proved in the pair are the index lemma and the loss of minimization past the first conjugate point; countable choice enters only through the declared suppliers.

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 10, printed p.189 immediately after Theorem 10.15: index of a geodesic segment and the Morse index theorem stated as a generalization the book does not treat.

items.title: Conjugate instants are isolated unless the geodesic is constant
items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used through [[lem-wronskian-of-two-jacobi-fields-is-constant]]. Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior, let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic, and fix $a\in I$. Define $$C_a(\gamma):=\{t\in I:t>a\text{ and }\gamma(a),\gamma(t)\text{ are conjugate along }\gamma|_{[a,t]}\}.$$ If $\gamma$ is nonconstant, then $C_a(\gamma)$ is discrete in $I\cap(a,\infty)$, and every compact subinterval of $I\cap(a,\infty)$ meets $C_a(\gamma)$ in finitely many points. If $\gamma$ is constant, then $C_a(\gamma)=\varnothing$. No completeness or full Axiom of Choice is assumed. At included endpoints, discreteness is relative to the parameter interval and derivatives are one-sided.

items.statement: Assuming AC_omega through the Riemann-tensor symmetry dependency: Let F(s,r,t) be an admissible two-parameter variation on a compact interval [a,b] with a<b, smooth on a common finite subdivision in t and smooth in (s,r) at the seams, whose central curve gamma(t)=F(0,0,t) is an affinely parametrized geodesic. Put E(s,r)=1/2 integral_a^b |F_t|^2 dt, V=F_s(0,0,.), W=F_r(0,0,.), T=gamma-dot. Then partial_s partial_r E(0,0)=integral_a^b (g(D_tV,D_tW)-g(R(V,T)T,W))dt+[g(D_sW,T)]_a^b. Equivalently, after piecewise integration by parts this is [g(D_sW,T)]_a^b+[g(D_tV,W)]_a^b-sum_j g(Delta_j D_tV,W(t_j))-integral_a^b g(D_t^2V+R(V,T)T,W)dt. Here Delta_j is the right-minus-left covariant-derivative jump. If endpoints are fixed, the acceleration term vanishes (and W(a)=W(b)=0 in the integrated form).

items.title: Index form of a geodesic segment
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega as propagated through the declared second-variation and Riemann-symmetry dependencies: Let a<b and let gamma:[a,b]->M be an affinely parametrized geodesic. Let X_pw^1(gamma) be the real vector space of continuous vector fields along gamma that are C1 on each piece of some finite subdivision, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. Define I_gamma(V,W)=integral_a^b (g(D_tV,D_tW)-g(R(V,gamma-dot)gamma-dot,W))dt, using finite piecewise Riemann integration. This is a symmetric bilinear form. Its fixed-endpoint subspace is X_0(gamma)={V in X_pw^1(gamma): V(a)=V(b)=0}. For every fixed-endpoint two-parameter variation with central gamma, the mixed energy derivative equals I_gamma(V,W).

items.title: Integration by parts for the index form
items.statement: Assume ACω as carried by the supplied index-form definition and def-countable-choice. Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold, a<b, and γ:[a,b]→M an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic. Fix a finite subdivision a=t₀<⋯<tₘ=b and continuous fields V,W along γ, with V C² and W C¹ on each closed piece. Define ΔⱼD_tV=D_tV(tⱼ⁺)−D_tV(tⱼ⁻). Then Iγ(V,W)=[g(D_tV,W)]ₐᵇ−Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ⁻¹g(ΔⱼD_tV,W(tⱼ))−Σₖ₌₁ᵐ∫ₜₖ₋₁ᵗₖg(D_t²V+R(V,T)T,W)dt, where T=γ̇ and the outer bracket uses one-sided endpoint traces. The finite-piece calculation adds no further choice assumption.

items.strategy: On each smooth piece, use metric compatibility to differentiate g(D_tV,W), apply Newton–Leibniz and linearity of the Riemann integral, then sum the boundary terms. Continuity of W makes each interior boundary contribution the negative pairing with the right-minus-left jump in D_tV; the resulting formula holds for every common finite subdivision.

items.title: Jacobi fields are the null solutions of the index form with fixed endpoints
items.statement: Assume ACω through the declared index-form dependencies. Let γ:[a,b]→M be an affinely parametrized geodesic with a<b, and let X²_pw(γ) be the continuous fields that are C² on every piece of some finite subdivision; set X²_0=X²_pw∩{V:V(a)=V(b)=0}. The radical of Iγ restricted to X²_0 is exactly the Jacobi fields with J(a)=J(b)=0. For any smooth Jacobi field J, Iγ(J,W)=0 for every unconstrained continuous piecewise-C¹ test field W if and only if D_tJ(a)=D_tJ(b)=0. Included endpoints use one-sided derivatives; constant geodesics and dimensions zero and one are included. No completeness is assumed.

items.title: Index lemma
items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited countable-choice axiom AC_omega. Let (M,g) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, a<b, and gamma:[a,b]->M an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic with T=gamma-dot. Assume that for no t in (a,b] are gamma(a),gamma(t) conjugate along gamma|[a,t]. Let u in T_{gamma(a)}M and w in T_{gamma(b)}M. Then (1) there is exactly one Jacobi field J along gamma with J(a)=u and J(b)=w; (2) for every continuous field V along gamma that is C^1 on the pieces of a finite subdivision and satisfies V(a)=u, V(b)=w, one has I_gamma(J,J)<=I_gamma(V,V), with equality if and only if V=J. Constant geodesics, dimension zero, u=w=0 and non-unit speed are included; no completeness, compactness or full AC.

items.strategy: The initial-value Jacobi map Phi_t(v)=J_v(t) is injective exactly because no conjugate instant exists, hence bijective by rank-nullity in equal dimension n; this solves the prescribed-endpoint problem uniquely. For V=J+W with W zero at both endpoints, integration by parts with the Jacobi equation cancels I(J,W). In a parallel frame the fields J_i=J_{E_i(a)} form a basis, W=A f, and the Wronskian identity <A-prime g, A h>=<A g, A-prime h> turns the integrand into <A f-prime, A f-prime> plus the exact derivative d/dt<A-prime f, A f>. Because A(t)=(t-a)(I+o(1)) and W(a)=0 the boundary term at a vanishes in the limit, so I(W,W)=integral of <A f-prime,A f-prime> >=0; equality forces f-prime=0, hence f constant and zero by W(b)=0.

items.title: H-one Riemannian curves and their half-energy
items.statement: Under AC_omega, on a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, an H1 curve on [a,b] is a continuous curve with a finite chart subdivision whose coordinate representatives are L2-derivative primitives; it has an a.e. tangent velocity, intrinsic L1 length and half-energy E=1/2 integral |alpha-dot|_g^2, and the H1 path topology implies uniform convergence. Smooth composition obeys the a.e. L2 chain rule.

items.title: Local length comparison for a conjugate-free geodesic
items.statement: Assume exactly the inherited countable-choice axiom AC_omega, propagated through the declared exponential-map, Jacobi-field and conjugacy suppliers. Let (M,g) be a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, let a<b, and let gamma:[a,b]->M be an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic such that for no t in (a,b] are gamma(a) and gamma(t) conjugate along gamma|[a,t]. Write p=gamma(a), v=gamma-dot(a), X=(b-a)v. Then there is a real epsilon>0 such that every continuous piecewise C^1 curve gamma-bar:[a,b]->M with gamma-bar(a)=gamma(a), gamma-bar(b)=gamma(b) and sup_t d_g(gamma-bar(t),gamma(t))<epsilon satisfies L_g(gamma-bar)>=L_g(gamma), and equality holds if and only if gamma-bar=gamma@tau for some continuous nondecreasing piecewise C^1 surjection tau:[a,b]->[a,b] with tau(a)=a and tau(b)=b. Constant geodesics are included; no completeness, unit speed, compactness of M or full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

items.strategy: The segment is covered by finitely many tangent balls on which exp_p is a diffeomorphism, using that d(exp_p) is invertible along the conjugate-free segment (a kernel vector would give a nonzero Jacobi field vanishing at both ends). A nearby curve is pulled back to a piecewise C^1 curve phi with exp_p@phi=gamma-bar; the smoothed radius sqrt(|phi|^2+sigma^2) satisfies the pointwise Gauss-lemma bound |gamma-bar-prime|>=|f_sigma-prime| on each strip, so Newton-Leibniz gives L(gamma-bar)>=sqrt(|X|^2+sigma^2)-sigma for every sigma>0, hence L(gamma-bar)>=L(gamma), with the sub-interval bound L(gamma-bar|[u,w])>=|r(w)-r(u)|. Equality forces the radius r to be bounded, nondecreasing and free of interior excursions, the tangential part of phi-prime to vanish, and the direction phi/r to be the constant direction X/|X|; then gamma-bar=gamma@tau with tau the radial reparametrization. Conversely a monotone reparametrization preserves length.

items.strategy: Use the finite exponential inverse branches from the local piecewise-C1 length comparison; smooth L2 superposition gives an H1 pullback. Apply Gauss lemma a.e. to smoothed radial norms, then dominated convergence and the zero-integral equality case to force the angular derivative to vanish and obtain a monotone radial reparametrization.

items.title: A geodesic segment before its first conjugate point is locally energy minimizing
items.statement: Under AC_omega, an affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic gamma:[a,b]->M, a<b, with no conjugate point to gamma(a) through b is a strict local half-energy minimizer among all fixed-endpoint H1 Riemannian curves: for some epsilon>0 every such alpha uniformly epsilon-close to gamma satisfies E(alpha)>=E(gamma), with equality iff alpha=gamma. This also holds in the H1 path topology, including constant geodesics, without completeness or compactness assumptions.

items.strategy: Use the H1 local length comparison and H1 half-energy definition. Holder gives E(alpha)>=L(alpha)^2/(2(b-a))>=E(gamma); equality in the first inequality is proved by expanding integral (speed-mean speed)^2 and applying zero-integral implies zero a.e., while equality in the second yields an AC nondecreasing H1 reparametrization alpha=gamma@tau. The a.e. smooth-composition chain rule and constant geodesic speed force tau-prime=1 a.e., hence the primitive identity gives tau=id. H1 embeds in C0, so the uniform radius supplies an H1 neighborhood.

items.title: A geodesic does not minimize past its first conjugate point
items.statement: Assume exactly the library’s countable-choice axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the declared exponential-map, index-form and second-variation interfaces. Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, let $a<c<b$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a nonconstant affinely parametrized Levi-Civita geodesic. If $\gamma(a)$ and $\gamma(c)$ are conjugate along $\gamma|_{[a,c]}$, then a piecewise smooth fixed-endpoint competitor on $[a,b]$ has both strictly smaller energy (for this fixed parameter interval) and strictly smaller length. No completeness or full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

items.strategy: Take a nonzero Jacobi field J on [a,c] with J(a)=J(c)=0 and cut it off as V=J on [a,c], V=0 after c. Initial-value uniqueness gives D_tJ(c^-)≠0. Choose the unique parallel section E on [a,b] with E(c)=-D_tJ(c^-), and set W(t)=((t-a)(b-t))/((c-a)(b-c)) E(t), so W(c)=-D_tJ(c^-) and W(a)=W(b)=0. The piecewise integration-by-parts identity gives I(V,V)=0 and I(V,W)=-|D_tJ(c^-)|^2. For a sufficiently small positive δ, X=V+δW has I(X,X)<0. Realize X by the explicit fixed-endpoint piecewise smooth variation β(s,t)=exp_{γ(t)}(sX(t)); compactness and openness of the exponential domain give one common parameter interval, including matching parameter derivatives at the seam. The differential of exp at the zero section is the identity, so β_s-field is X. First variation gives E′(0)=0, second variation gives E″(0)=I(X,X)<0, and the second-derivative test yields E(β_s)<E(γ) for small nonzero s. Since γ has constant speed, L(γ)^2=2(b-a)E(γ); the length-energy inequality gives L(β_s)^2≤2(b-a)E(β_s)<L(γ)^2. This direct argument is local and needs no completeness.

items.title: At a conjugate endpoint the index form is degenerate
items.statement: Assume exactly AC_omega through the declared dependencies. (a) If gamma(a) and gamma(b) are conjugate along an affinely parametrized geodesic gamma:[a,b]->M (a<b, finite-dimensional boundaryless), then the fixed-endpoint index form on X_0(gamma) is degenerate: some nonzero J in X_0(gamma) satisfies I_gamma(J,W)=0 for every W in X_0(gamma). (b) On the round sphere S_R^n (R>0, n>=2), for p and unit v, gamma(t)=exp_p(tv) on [0,pi R] ends at -p, is minimizing with d(p,-p)=L(gamma)=pi R, but is not a strict local minimizer: for every epsilon>0 there is a piecewise C^1 path sigma != gamma from p to -p with L(sigma)=pi R and sup_t d(sigma(t),gamma(t))<epsilon. The fixed-endpoint index form is degenerate with nullspace exactly the endpoint-vanishing Jacobi fields, of dimension n-1.

items.title: Unit spheres in finite-dimensional normed spaces are sequentially compact
items.statement: No choice principle is used. Let V be a finite-dimensional real normed space with unit sphere S = {v in V : ||v|| = 1}. Then S is sequentially compact: every sequence in S has a subsequence converging in the norm metric to a point of S. Consequently, for a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) and p in M, the unit sphere S_pM = {v in T_pM : |v|_g = 1} is sequentially compact, so every sequence of unit tangent vectors at p has a subsequence converging in the norm metric of T_pM to a unit tangent vector at p. Dimension zero and dimension one are included.
items.strategy: The closed unit ball of a finite-dimensional normed space is compact because a finite basis gives a coordinate isomorphism; compactness passes to countably compact and then sequentially compact subspaces, and the limit of a sequence of unit vectors is again a unit vector by the reverse triangle inequality.

items.title: Characterization of a cut point
items.statement: Assume exactly the countable-choice axiom AC_omega. Let (M,g) be a complete, connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, p in M, v in S_pM a unit tangent vector, gamma(t)=exp_p(tv), and c=c_p(v) in (0,+infinity] the cut time. (a) Forward: if c<infinity, then either gamma(0)=p and gamma(c) are conjugate along gamma|[0,c], or there is a unit-speed minimizing geodesic sigma:[0,c]->M with sigma(0)=p, sigma(c)=gamma(c) and sigma'(0)!=v, so two distinct minimizing geodesics join p to gamma(c) in time c. (b) Converse: (1) if t>0 and gamma(0),gamma(t) are conjugate along gamma|[0,t], then c<=t; (2) if a unit-speed minimizing sigma:[0,t]->M with sigma(0)=p, sigma(t)=gamma(t) and sigma'(0)!=v exists, then c<=t. Hence for finite c, c is the least positive instant at which one of the two forward alternatives occurs. Dimension zero is vacuous (no unit tangent vector); gamma is nonconstant because |v|_g=1.

Conversely, conjugacy at t gives a strictly shorter competitor past t, and a second unit-speed minimizer makes the concatenated broken path globally shortest, so its arclength representative is an unbroken geodesic and velocity uniqueness forces the two geodesics to coincide.

items.title: Cut time is positive and continuous

Dimension zero is vacuous and no compactness of M is assumed.
